speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-REMOVAL OF COAT OF ARMS FROM PUBLICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, some ten days ago I raised a question on the omission of the coat of arms from the new Standing Orders of the house. Of course I realize I am not permitted to ask Your Honour any questions, but I would appreciate it if it could be made clear as to whether an examination by Your Honour has been made of the question that I raised, and what will be the position from now on of the coat of arms on the publication of Standing Orders.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-REMOVAL OF COAT OF ARMS FROM PUBLICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Order, please. The right hon. gentleman knows what the rules are in so far as the Chair is concerned. The only way that questions can be asked is in writing. There has been a communication in writing with the right hon. gentleman and it was my hope that the answer which was conveyed to him would be satisfactory.
I think that there should be as few exceptions as possible to the rule, because it is a good rule, that communications with the Speaker in so far as inquiries are concerned should be made in writing, and the reply made in the same way by the Chair. If the house will allow the Speaker, however, to make an exception to the rule, I will say that the intention of the officers of the house and of the Speaker is that eventually when the Standing Orders are published in this final form they will be published in the traditional way which has always been observed in the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-REMOVAL OF COAT OF ARMS FROM PUBLICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
The coat of arms will come back then.

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES. 1969-70 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD

speechtext: A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1970, was presented by Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board), and read by Mr. Speaker to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board):
maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES. 1969-70 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budgetary estimates for 1969-70 total $11,858 million. Normal lapsing would bring expenditures based on these estimates down to something below the $11,670 million figure projected by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in his budget speech last October. The 1969-70 budgetary estimates of $11,858 million compare with anticipated total 1968-69 estimates of $10,826 million. The increase between years is, therefore, $1,032 million. Of this increase, $859 million relate to statutory items and the balance, or $173 million, to items requiring annual appropriations.
It should be recalled that the Minister of Finance has mentioned on several occasions that expenditures could easily vary from the projection of $11,670 million by about 1 per cent either way. In this connection I should point out that while these estimates were being printed the provincial governments were asked to provide us with more up-to-date forecasts of their expenditures under the Canada Assistance Plan, the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, and for post-secondary education. These latest forecasts confirm the validity of the total amount included in the estimates tabled today for these programs. It is not possible for me to be more definite in this report, since most provincial treasuries are still in the process of preparing their own 1969-70 estimates, which will not be presented to their legislatures for some weeks yet.
There may be a need, as in the past, for supplementary estimates in the course of the year to meet urgent and unforeseen requirements. The government is determined that

February 4, 1969
Main Estimates 1969-70 such supplementary estimates, if any, will be kept to a minimum and held to figures consistent with the declared objective of a balanced budget.
The estimates make provision for the expenditures required under programs for which statutory authority has already been granted by specific acts of parliament, such as the large programs already mentioned, as well as medicare and public debt charges, or resulting from formal agreements with the provinces such as those relating to occupational training of adults, and regional development. It should be noted that in respect to medicare, as indicated in the budget speech, provision has been made on the basis of participation by all the provinces for the full year.
Apart from these outlays, which are not readily manageable in the short term at least, the estimates for 1969-70 provide the required funds for the government to carry out its current defence commitments, and reflect the decision of the government to give priority to a number of specific areas of activity within an over-all framework of budgetary restraint.
Increased allocations have been made to programs for the efficient growth of the economy; to measures that contribute to raising the level of industrial technology, research and development and improving productivity; to programs for the support of research in the universities, and to water research programs.
Growth has also been provided in programs essential to the strengthening of national unity; to the reduction of regional disparities; to the improvement of the situation of Indians and Eskimos, and to the expansion of our external aid.
Finally, provision has been made to meet the increasing needs of parliament and essential funds have been allowed for the protection of persons and property, toward the acquisition of a communications satellite, and for postal operations.
A careful scrutiny was carried out of the manpower requirements of the various departments and agencies of the public service with the result, shown at page 476 of the estimates blue book, that the over-all manpower allocation for the year 1969-70 shows a decrease of 9,332 man-years from the levels authorized in the current year. The program of restraint on the over-all size of the public service which was announced by the government in March 1968 will be continued in 1969-70.
The considerations outlined above are reflected in the major elements of increase in the 1969-70 estimates over those of the current year. About 83 per cent of the over-all increase is made up of the requirements for programs authorized by existing legislation such as: medicare, $335 million; superannuation-civil and R.C.M.P., $154 million; public debt charges, $130 million; fiscal transfers to the provinces, $101 million; hospital insurance payments, $65 million; post-secondary education payments, $53 million; superannuation- defence, $51 million; Canada Assistance Plan, $48 million.
In the category of programs for which annual appropriations of parliament are required and which account for $6,185 million or 52 per cent of the total, the major elements of increase are: defence services, $51 million; regional economic expansion contributions, $46 million; federal government accommodation, $35 million; adult occupational training, $34 million, Indian, Eskimo and northern development programs, $33 million; external aid (excluding loans), $18 million; broadcasting, $15 million; grants for scientific and social research, $14 million; postal services, $13 million; industrial development assistance, $7 million; water research programs, $5 million.
The foregoing amounts relating to budgetary expenditures do not include loans, investments and advances on non-budgetary account, for which parliamentary approval is also being sought, in the amount of $614 million in the 1969-70 estimates. The corresponding amount in total estimates for 1968-69 is $720 million.
Similarly, the budgetary expenditures set forth in the preceding paragraphs do not include the forecast expenditures for Old Age Security payments. These payments, amounting to an estimated $1,760 million in 1969-70 -compared to $1,581 million in 1968-69-are carried separately from the budgetary expenditures provided for in the estimates as a statutory charge against the Old Age Security fund to which are credited the special taxes levied for this purpose.
I should also point out that a few presentational changes have been introduced in the 1969-70 blue book of estimates. For the first time we are providing details of the estimates requirements of crown corporations. Further, we have simplified the presentation of manpower detail and introduced a new standard expenditure coding system.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PERCENTAGE DISTRIBUTION OF BUDGETARY EXPENDITURES BY MAJOR FUNCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time I wish to make two or three comments on the estimates. I have just received them and heard the minister's remarks, and I think they are worthy of a little more study than I have been able to give them so far. Therefore I will not attempt to make extensive comments. Yet I could not help noting that the minister's remarks seemed to be delivered in an apologetic way. That may have been a personal impression, but it is an impression, nevertheless, that struck me very definitely.
I notice that the estimates are increased by $1.32 billion over the revised estimates for last year, in round figures an increase of 10 per cent. That increase contrasts sharply with a conviction expressed by the former minister of finance a little over a year ago that the estimates would not be increased by more than 4.5 per cent. At any rate, the increase in estimates was to be confined to that percentage. The actual percentage of the increase is double that fixed, so to speak, by the former minister of finance. The undertaking of the previous minister was guaranteed, of course, by the present Minister of Finance.
We will, of course, study these estimates carefully. Nevertheless, because of our experience during the past year, we will take them with a grain of salt.

maintopic: PERCENTAGE DISTRIBUTION OF BUDGETARY EXPENDITURES BY MAJOR FUNCTION
speechtext: A whole bag full.

maintopic: PERCENTAGE DISTRIBUTION OF BUDGETARY EXPENDITURES BY MAJOR FUNCTION
speechtext:
We shall do so, particularly, since the minister sprinkled salt on the budget estimates when he said he was in no position to be particularly firm on estimates of joint cost programs.
It is also a matter of regret to me that these estimates are not being presented to the house in a context of satisfactory financial relations between the federal government and the provinces. There ought, at least, to be an apparent willingness on the part of the federal government to meet with the provinces and frankly to work out with them priorities and approaches that would be in the interest of the Canadian taxpayer. Therefore it is a matter of regret to me, and to most Canadians I think, that the atmosphere existing between the federal government and the provinces in the realm of financial relations is not good.
It will be the duty of the opposition, sir, to examine these estimates with care. This we will do in the light of experience we have had in the past year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I remember when other estimates were tabled. The present estimates are much like the others and reflect a stale likeness, as if the merit of any set of estimates is to be judged by how well the figures on both sides of the ledger balance. Any bookkeeper can make figures balance.
We concede that it is necessary for the government to run its operation on a businesslike basis, yet any businessman would be appalled at the government's attitude. After all, any business seeks to expand, to make use of initiative and seek out new avenues of opportunity. The present government does not seem to be prepared to act that way. It is perfectly content to demonstrate that the figures on one side of the ledger balance the other side.
We in this party look forward to the day when we will have a government that takes some of the actions that members in our society in the past have taken. It takes the attitude that this is a country that needs governing and leadership, that has an exciting future and deserves far more than a flat assessment of the debits and credits as given to us today. We look forward to the day when that will take place.

maintopic: PERCENTAGE DISTRIBUTION OF BUDGETARY EXPENDITURES BY MAJOR FUNCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister who has just presented the budgetary estimates for the year ending March 31st, 1970 speaks of the importance of a balanced budget. Now, in order to achieve this, restrictions have been made, as usual, in every sphere of Canadian economic activity while the physical possibilities of developing the wealth of our country have been completely overlooked.
Mr. Speaker, I am anxious to see a responsible minister rise in this house to speak to us not only of a budget which enables us to spend the taxes levied but of a balanced budget which would take into account the potential resources of Canada and would make everything financially possible, according to the theory we advocate, throughout Canada, in short wherever we go, that is to make financially possible what is physically achievable.
Mr. Speaker, I note in those estimates that the interest on the national debt this year will amount to $1,604,000,000. Although that item increases from year to year, the minister

We go visiting countries throughout the world trying to help them, while we cannot even take steps to help the Canadian people who develop or are willing to develop the natural resources of our country. If that is what is called a just society, it is indeed a strange just society. Mr. Speaker, some days ago I undertook to make a brief statement with respect to the limitations on air crews serving on our regular air lines. The physical and mental condition of flight crew is a matter of continuing concern to governments all over the world. For this reason m the late 1940's ICAO, the International Civil Aviation Organization, recommended that member states take action to establish limitations on the flight time of flight crew members in the interests of flight safety. This ICAO recommendation was accepted by Canada and minimum standards in keeping with the ICAO recommendation were formulated with the assistance of the aviation industry associations concerned. Because of the variety of aircraft operations in Canada to which such standards must apply, the standards adopted were, of necessity, general in nature.
Over the years they have had to be amended slightly to meet specific situations, but it can be said that, notwithstanding a recognized need to refine them to take full accou t of individual types of operation, they have been given general acceptance by operators and crews alike.
In the application of these standards the Department of Transport requires every operator of large aircraft engaged in commercial air operations to submit a proposed text to the department for approval, for inclusion in the company's approved operations manual setting out instructions in this regard for compliance by company personnel. In considering the acceptability of such proposals the department takes into account environmental factors involved, such as the length of route stages, weather, type of aircraft, number of landings and take-offs, etc., as well as the consistency of the proposal with the standard itself. The acceptability of such a proposal is an important prerequisite to the over-all safety certification of the operator.
As an example the flight time limitations approved for Air Canada's operations limit flight crews to a maximum of 85 hours per month, 14 hours in any one day including the time necessary to prepare for and terminate a flight. There is also a requirement for a minimum rest period of eight hours between duty periods during which the crews are relieved of all duties associated with their employment.

Some concern has been expressed aibout the length of time spent on duty by Air Canada crews on the Montreal-Moscow service. In this regard I can say that the maximum duty time on the Montreal-Moscow service is 9j hours.
While the procedures now followed in establishing flight time limitations through the approval of the company operations manual have served the purpose for which they were intended, future developments in aviation will require more scientific methods for determining fatigue levels. To this end the Department of Transport is participating in a study by MpGill University. The Federal Aviation Agency of the United States also has a study under way. Depending on the outcome of these studies the department will take whatever action is necessary in the circumstances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this additional cash advance to assist in drying damp grain is another indication that the government failed to recognize the problem which began to develop last fall. It failed to bring forth measures soon enough in order to alleviate the difficulty which was apparent as early as last October. The government has now made a belated effort to shift the responsibility for drying the grain from the terminals which have customarily done the drying for the farmers.
The problem of damp grain arose in 1959 and again since that time. Mr. McNamara, the head of the Wheat Board, has said until very recently in any event that farmers must use a great deal of caution in tire use of driers on their farms'because of the danger of burning or cooking the wheat which would ruin thq protein content and make it lower than our export standards. In the last few weeks the Wheat Board has published full-page ads in weekly papers advising farmers that they should dry and not fry their wheat. The government is encouraging the farmers to dry their grain rather than consolidate it and have it dried commercially either at the terminals or on the prairies. It has said it will give the farmer a cash advance of 10 cents a bushel, but it is not giving the farmers anything but the interest. That is all. The bill is not clear on the point whether the cash advance is over and above the allowable six bushel quota cash advance which many farmers may have at the present time. If it is, it is still not enough.
Debate regarding the damp grain has arisen in the house from time to time throughout the winter. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) in his last speech scolded the opposition for attempting to make headlines. He said that the net effect of debating this question in

Mr. Speaker, I was tempted to speak in this debate last Friday but was under the impression that there was agreement to pass the legislation that day and I did not want to deprive opposition spokesmen of the opportunity of speaking. It seems a little strange to me that many hon. members opposite should at the beginning or during their speeches indicate their support of this measure and then proceed to talk about other matters in connection with agriculture and delay its passage. A little delay in the implementation of this emergency cash advance legislation is not really very serious, however. The main thing is that the farmers should know it will be forthcoming before spring. This has been known to most of us ever since the government announced some weeks ago its intention to provide this special form of assistance.
There has been some criticism of this method of providing cash to help farmers pay the cost of drying their grain. Certainly some farmers and farm organizations requested outright cash assistance. This would have been the popular way to do it, and I am sure most people would prefer a grant to a loan if they had a choice. Some farmers in western Canada have been saying, though, that it IMr. Horner.]

would be unfair to make cash payments to farmers who had damp grain, giving nothing to those thousands of farmers whose crops were reduced in yield, quality and value by frost, drought or hail. Many farmers with damp grain also have other grain that may have been harvested dry, or has been carried over from last year. Many have livestock and poultry. Very few are destitute and seeking charity.
It has been alleged that by using this method of providing assistance the government is getting off scot-free so far as the unusual, emergency damp grain situation which exists on the prairies is concerned. I point out that these cash advances are interest free to the farmers but not to the government. I ask hon. members to remember that the amount of cash advances was doubled last fall, anc with these special advances the government will now be putting up a very substantial sum of money by way of interest and carrying charges on loans, some of which will not be fully repaid for many, many months.

We know that the government has not abandoned us. We know that much legislation regarding agriculture has been presented this session. We know that cash advances have been doubled, that farm improvement loans have been reactivated, and more capital has been made available to the Farm Credit Corporation. We know that the government recently put the Wheat Board on a permanent basis. Mr. Speaker, this bill is a pretence and a farce. In my view it is a substitute for action. It is one more illustration of the government's inability and unwillingness to take effective steps to deal with a crisis which is much more than a farm crisis or a western crisis. What we face here is a national crisis which has already taken its toll and will cost the Canadian economy much more if effective measures are not taken immediately.
Let me give the house some examples of the effect of this situation to date on various sectors of the Canadian economy. Take a look at retail sales in Saskatchewan. In the most recent six months for which figures are available, that is, from May to October, a period which predates the immediate crisis, retail sales in Saskatchewan amounted to $540.5 million, a drop of about $7.6 million compared with the figure for the same six months in 1967. If one takes into account the inflationary factor of approximately 4 per cent it means that the comparable figure for 1967 would be about $570 million, which would produce an effective drop in retail sales of some $30 million or over 5 per cent. There is little doubt, I believe, that this decline in retail sales will continue in the province, with an adverse effect both on the economy of Saskatchewan and on the economy of Canada as a whole. I suggest that all hon. members in

this house should be concerned about the consequences of this situation.
As another example I draw attention to the situation in which auto dealers in Regina find themselves. They have experienced a decline of between 40 and 50 per cent in their car sales compared with a year ago. This, of course, has a direct effect on the automobile industry and will be of immediate concern to hon. members from Windsor, Oshawa, Hamilton and Oakville. Sales of farm equipment are also falling considerably below those of a year ago and this, in turn, has a serious effect upon the farm machinery industry.
When he introduced this bill on Friday the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) really had very little to say. I note, however, that he did use the following words:

Mr. Speaker, I shall be quite brief. I say without any reservation that I support this bill. I think it is a good bill. I should like to make three points. I think hon. members on both sides will agree that all news media- newspaper, television or radio-in a democracy are part of that democracy. After all, it is the news that is published which causes the public to be informed concerning what parliament and the government are doing. In fact you can carry this to any extent so far as a democracy is concerned. In a democracy it is the responsibility of the press to report the facts.
Some people may suggest that over the years there has been some change in reporting in that the reporters now act more as column writers, commentators and artists who paint the news as they see it rather than print the facts so that the people can draw their own inferences. I believe, however, we must accept that the newspaper is a very important part of the functioning of any parliamentary system. All one need do is think of any European country which has established a dictatorship to realize that those dictatorships control the press. The people

there are fed the kind of information the dictator and the group around him want the people to have. We have seen the invasion recently of Czechoslovakia. We know that when the U.S.S.R. took over that country their first attempt was to control the press in order to hide from the people there the real issues and the views of their leader so far as liberty and freedom are concerned. So on this basis I support the bill.
Ini order to obtain news-and this is where I fall out with the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Gibson)-the press must have sources. The great news stories of the world come from certain sources. If those sources must be disclosed then the tap of news dries up. I have always felt that a medical man should have the same privilege a solicitor has. If someone discloses information to a solicitor that information is privileged; it cannot be given in evidence in court. The solicitor can apply for the privilege and it will be given. This does not apply to medical men. I think, however, that this privilege should apply to the press. For instance, if I personally happened to be the source of information I might not in that particular case wish my name to be connected with the story.
If we were to say that the names of people must be disclosed we would dry up the news; we would close the tap and shut off the flow of truth to the nation. I support the bill wholeheartedly. I believe that when the members of the committee take a look at it they will appreciate that as the hon. member suggested there is a protection under this bill. When one speaks of slander and libel, nowhere in this bill is there anything which prevents the newspaper or the reporter being sued for libel or slander.

Mr. Speaker, I endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and I approve wholeheartedly this legislation involving some basic matters.
To approve such legislation is simply to approve freedom because in this day and age a free press or the freedom of the press is synonymous with a free nation. The press having become above all a most important and even essential means to ensure a well functioning democracy, it follows that we must protect at all costs those who, by their actions or their role as journalists, promote true freedom. We can only rejoice that such a bill was introduced, which if passed will give well deserved protection to those dedicated people, as they sometimes sacrifice themselves for freedom. I will give an example. A couple of months ago, some articles published in the Montreal newspaper La Presse, were excerpts from Volume 3 of the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission report on bilingualism and biculturalism. If La Presse had not had access to this source of information, we may never have been informed of what was written in a certain chapter of that volume, and this at the public's expense, because if we compel those who obtained that information to divulge their source, they will never again have access to it.
Quite often, we realize that information originates almost exclusively from the press, and we, on this side of the house, have often complained that the press knew the facts ahead of us, even in cases involving parliamentary prerogatives.
If news sources are good only when one is In power, I cannot see why a distinction should be made in other circumstances, because since the reporter has to play an essential part in our society, he must enjoy full liberty of action.
As pointed out by the hon. member who spoke before me, it goes without saying that if a reporter, in order to get information, breaks the law of the country, then he runs the risk of being prosecuted, and he will have deserved it.
The question here is to protect him, by not compelling him to disclose his news sources.
To follow up the instance I have just given, I was saying that an editorial in the Montreal newspaper La Presse had even blamed the R.C.M.P. for checking up the

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has introduced this afternoon, Bill C-15 concerning a very important matter which can be connected with the main question of the privileges or the freedom of the press.
It is a matter which in history has given rise to interesting debates and even to several epoch making cases. It is a burning issue because thanks to the technical development of present media, news reach an ever increasing number of people.
However, I am sorry that the hon. member for Timiskaming and the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) dealt so little with the principle of the bill which, I understand, does not attack the question of the freedom of the press in general, but simply aims at providing privilege of communication between a journalist and his news source or in respect of his source where the source is a document or other material, on the occasion of proceedings under the federal authority.
However, the hon. member took unfair advantage of it, thus transgressing the rules, to attack the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). In fact, his reference to the London incident constitutes, in my opinion, a case where it can be said that there has been misuse of the freedom of the press in that the latter did not act exactly as it should have, regarding the privacy of people.
On the other hand, the hon. member for Calgary North also took that opportunity to speak of the freedom of the press and of what happened, for instance, in the countries behind the iron curtain or in Germany before the last World War, when the press was controlled.
I do not think it is intended in this bill to put any limitations on the freedom of the press which must remain independent and impartial. I would like to deal more specifically with the purpose of the bill which would entitle a journalist, when sued for defamatory libel, for instance, or for something else concerning perhaps the security of the country, the private life or the reputation
DEBATES	5135
News Sources Protection Act of a citizen not to divulge his news source. And I think this is the matter the hon. member wished to put before the house this afternoon.
However, press privileges-what we call the freedom of the press-include of course the right for a reporter to gather, as he sees fit and practically without any limits, information he may broadcast thereafter, and this bill provides for a communication privilege between the journalist and his news source in any proceedings conducted before criminal or federal courts. In fact, if we consider the bill, we notice that it goes far enough, because the definition applies to, and I quote:
-a criminal proceeding held before or under the authority of a court exercising judicial authority-
The bill goes on as follows:
-an inquiry or investigation held or made under authority of a law of Canada or by order of Her Majesty before or under the authority of a court, tribunal, commission, board, power, authority, or a judicial, administrative or ministerial official, or any other proceeding or matter whatsoever coming within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada or within the prerogative of Her Majesty;-
When we look at the definition of "journalist" or "newspaper", we see that it includes not only the written news, but also radio, television, etc.
This is therefore a bill that goes quite far, but during a trial for libel, for instance, where the private rights of a citizen may be involved, should a journalist who has free scope to publish information obtained by him, be considered as a preferred witness, under no obligation to disclose his news source, when he appears before the court? I think that an entirely new situation would be created.
As the hon. member must know, the courts have always in the past, except in cases where national security was threatened, compelled newspaper men to disclose their news sources. The right to conceal news sources has never been considered a privilege comparable, for example, with that of a lawyer and his client, as pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary North who wanted to put the newspaper man on an equal footing with the lawyer.
Now, some distinctions can surely be made between the two and I ask the following question: Does the newspaper men have more rights than the ordinary citizens before the law or should they enjoy an exceptional status, as for example, the one existing
February 4, 1969

News Sources Protection Act between husband and wife or that enjoyed by the counsel for the defence in a criminal court?
In my opinion, the scope of the freedom of the press can be restricted by the exercise of other liberties, by the basic rights of other citizens, in order to assure a better administration of justice.
I am thinking particularly of the rights of the ordinary citizens when his reputation is involved or in order that his private life be respected. In the present case, a newspaper man would have the privilege of not being compelled to disclose in the proceedings listed in the bill his source of information for news and reports on events of public interest which are published or broadcast.
As a result of the proposed legislation, a reporter could refuse to answer a question, or to produce a document which would disclose his news source. The right to invoke this privilege would be given to the reporter alone, and not to his source of information, and it seems that it would be impossible to ask why he refuses to testify.
In law, apart from some exceptions I have mentioned earlier and which are well specified in statutes, the general rule is that any person can be a competent witness and can be forced to reveal the names of those who gave him the information according to which the article was written.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The Criminal Code and the Evidence Act grant this privilege to certain people such as the accused, for instance, who is not obliged to testify at his own trial or at the trial of his wife, subject to some exceptions when the accused could get protection should he incriminate himself by his answer. He can then ask for the protection of the court, so that his answer could not be used as evidence in future procedures; however, he cannot refuse to answer. The privilege is also extended to the lawyer and his client-and it is understandable-since the obligation for any able person to testify during judicial procedures on relevant facts known to him, is justified by the fact that it is the best way to get full justice and that it gives the courts the possibility to judge with complete knowledge of the facts. That is why the administration of justice imposes this obligation.
As a matter of fact, I think that the authors have established rules which are considered essential towards recognizing that privilege of not being compelled to disclose to the court 
certain information, and the four following rules are set forth:
(1)	The communication must proceed from the assurance that it will not be disclosed.
(2)	That assurance must be essential to the complete and satisfactory maintenance of relations between the parties.
(3)	The relation must be one which the community is interested to protect.
(4)	The adverse effect that the disclosure of the communication could have on the relation must be greater than the benefits which could ensue from the disclosure of the said communication in case of conflict.
These are the rules taught by the authors in order that the fact of not disclosing certain information may constitute a privilege before the court. When one thinks particularly of the relations which could exist between say a lawyer and his client, one sees that in such a case the rules are obviously adhered to. If, for example, a lawyer were to testify in a trial, that would more or less amount to saying that the client would be compelled indirectly to testify against himself. The same principles are involved in the case of the relations between husband and wife.
However, if we look closely at those rules, we realize that they do not apply at all in the case of a journalist who appears as a witness and who can be compelled to disclose his sources of information; he cannot benefit from those rules which are based on past experience.
The hon. member alluded to the case of Mr. Blair Fraser-whom several members have known and who unfortunately is dead-who had been involved in a lawsuit that created a great stir. He was sued by the Attorney General of British Columbia who had brought an action for damage against that journalist and the magazine who had published such information.
However, the precedents which were mentioned but that unfortunately I have not had the time to study thoroughly, refer particularly to the British jurisprudence. The Court's decision was that the journalist would have to reply to the questions. This judgment was based on a very elaborate jurisprudence. He appealed from the judgment of the Appeal Court of British Columbia which had upheld the judgment of the court of first instance, and the authorization to appeal to the Supreme Court was rejected. This case is referred to in the 4th volume of the Dominion Law Reports for 1954. Here is what one of the
February 4, 1969

Justices said; and I am quoting from page 334:
In the present case, in my opinion, the refusal of the defender to divulge the source of his information is sheer stubbornness. He has persisted for more than one year in his refusal to obey the orders of this country's courts. Now, he is more or less telling us that, after careful consideration, he believes his moral obligations towards the people who gave him the information are more important that his duty to obey the judgment of the Court.
Under these circumstances-
-as pointed out by another Justice-
-he must realize that his refusal brings about as a consequence the result achieved by the rules.
Well, it was decided that in a civil proceeding resulting from a libellous information published in a newspaper, the newsman had to answer questions. In this case, English jurisprudence was studied, where perhaps it seems to grant the privilege that the hon. member wishes to grant to the newspapers, but which does not extend to newsmen. In Canada, no decision was taken on this matter, but it was mentioned that the newspaperman in this case had to reveal his source of information.
Mr. Speaker, the bill presented by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) may, at first sight, seem to be of some advantage. But if we consider it in relation to its consequences, especially for certain persons who might be involved by newspapersmen's charges-and we know that newsmen sometimes go a bit too far-I submit that the freedom of the press must also be limited by other freedoms: that of individuals, in particular, and I am unable to support the principle of the bill because it goes a little too far.

Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was saying that there had been repeated remarks on the opposition as well as on the government side and that some government members, taking their role seriously or assuming their responsibilities had sometimes blamed the government for not acting in time. However, to stir up the sense of responsibility of the Minister of Agriculture in that field we had to have the emergency debate about a week ago, that somewhat clarified the question.
The object of Bill C-162 is to empower the government to grant advance payments to grain producers to enable them to better finance the drying of damp grain and provide storage otherwise than in an elevator.


I suggest that this legislation could have been more generous. However, it could not have changed the weather in any way. The government members say: Well, everything depends upon the weather; there was too much rain in the fall and this winter, the weather is too cold. Indeed, such things are not controlled by the government but from above. The Progressive Conservative members said to the government: You have failed to act m time. That is the reason why they asked the government to grant them cash in advance to enable them to afford the costs of drying the grain and of putting it into the elevators so that the ships would not leave Vancouver half empty. The government did absolutely nothing and grain deterioriated in the field and the grain piles on the prairies grew higher. The strike was followed by inaction on the part of the government with regard to the problem of drying grain. There were no incentives, no encouragement or no co-operation in the handling of driers and a 3 bushel quota of damp grain in effect plugged every available storage facility without consideration being given to the drying capacity available.
The Japanese are now demanding indemnities because of damp and second quality grain. They are also demanding compensation for ships tied up for days in Vancouver harbour. This is because the government failed to do anything about the moving of box cars. Many of my own neighbours have had their incomes cut in half because of the government's refusal to take any action in this serious situation. It is a tragedy and a damaging blow to Canada's economy that a large part of an entire year's grain crops and sales have been sacrificed because of bureaucratic bungling. The government refused to move to organize rail facilities to transport wheat to Vancouver. They failed to get the right grade to the right place at the right time. While millions of dollars in wheat went begging in Canada, box cars which should have been available were out of the country picking up a few bucks for the railways. If the railways are going to act in this manner, then they must be brought to task by the government, and that means a government capable of doing the job. The present government is more concerned with questions of manners and morals than the livelihood of the western farmer. Little wonder farmers all across western Canada are sick at heart at the way the situation is being handled.
Many farm leaders have expressed concern with regard to difficulties the farmers will experience in 1969, such as the rising cost of operation, loss of markets and loss of reasonable return due to deterioration of their grain caused by climatic conditions. Mr. Speaker, 1969 is here and, believe me, it is difficult on the prairies. Business is lagging, unemployment is rising, automobile and machinery sales are down, accounts receivable are running at an all-time high and becoming stagnant. Above all an ever-growing lack of confidence is being experienced in the future of farming and business enterprise. What about the future? According to Japanese reports, 117,000 tons of Manitoba No. 2 wheat contracted for December and January have not arrived in Tokyo. Can any country run its business that way? This government has allowed the Wheat Board to float by itself and to carry the whole load. The government has not helped or supported the board in any way. It was too concerned with its abortion bill. Surely, it is time we got back to the real 

things of life. Canada cannot tolerate disruptive mismanagement on the part of the federal government. Certainly the provincial governments will not tolerate this for any length of time.

Seven Japanese ships, among the 30 odd ships waiting in the Port of Vancouver, got sick of waiting. The Japanese, as we know, are no fools. They are the smartest businessmen in the Orient. They have taken a great interest in Canada, and have invested a lot of money here. The Japanese are prepared to buy our wheat, but they insist on the same high standards which they follow in their own affairs and if we do not deliver they will shop elsewhere, as they are now doing in Australia.
There has never been a time when the affairs of the western farmer have been more poorly managed by the government. The government simply let a whole year's grain crop drift away and we wonder if this is going to keep on because, if it does, then the western farmer will be in the same position as the eastern farmer. The policy announced by the government for the eastern farmer is to take him off the farm and put him in the welfare office in the city. The western farmer does not want that and will fight for his right to enjoy the prosperity he has created by his own sweat.
We have witnessed a whole year's crop flushed down the drain by Ottawa mismanagement. Here it is February and the government has finally managed to persuade the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) to go to Vancouver. It is too late to do much this year. We have been witnessing events which have sadly shaken the faith of farmers all across Canada.
Certainly all hon. members welcome the fact that the minister is now concerned. I enumerate these points in order that the Minister of Agriculture may realize that he will not get away with the remarks he has made about this emergency, namely, that his government is the only one that has done anything in situations like this.

The next problem is the lapse of the international wheat agreement and the loss of grain sales, with resulting low incomes to farmers so they have been unable to finance the drying of a large quantity of wet grain. This has been one of our major problems. The catastrophe facing western Canada results in part from the lapsing of the international wheat agreement which has created serious financial difficulties in our part of the country.
As members from the west know, we are plagued with large surpluses of dry grain in storage. This has been caused by the inaction and indifference of the government at the Kennedy round of talks at Geneva two years ago. I was interested in listening to the comments of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas), my neighbour in western Canada, who was trying to paint a bright picture out of the very dim one that we have out there. I do not blame him for that; it is his prerogative and, I suppose, his duty because he is a member of the party which forms the government.
He referred to the fact that last year we had a 25 per cent increase in sales over the previous year. But it must be remembered that we had last year only 30 per cent of the sales we had the year before. Therefore, an increase of 25 per cent last year is really an increase of only ri\ per cent, or a quarter of the 30 per cent. This is a very meagre increase and does not solve the problem at all. We have to go out and make wheat sales if we are to solve the basic problem underlying western agriculture.
I bring these facts to the attention of the house just to keep the record straight. We have heard a great deal about the Grains Council; the minister made an announcement about it on motions today. This is all well and good, and naturally I will support anything that will help to develop, maintain and continue the maintenance of sound agricultural policy in this country. But I am afraid this council will be only window dressing if it is to meet just once or twice a year and has on it people already involved in the grain trade.
I cannot for the life of me, and I hope I am wrong, see what the council will achieve in these circumstances. The council should use its influence, I suggest, to immediately try to reconvene the International Grains Council so that the international wheat agreement can be put back on the rails. It is all well and good to say the agreement has been re-established, but we are not deriving any benefit from it;

our competitors are selling their grain and we are sitting back with our bins full of grain.
My fourth point is that the order of the Wheat Board opening up a three-bushel quota on wet grain to terminals has created great difficulty in agriculture. It has choked up our drying facilities for three months and eliminated all possibility of moving dry grain into position to meet world market demands. The question is, who demanded that the Wheat Board take this action? Was it the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), or the Minister of Agriculture? Surely, it was not the Wheat Board alone that decided to make this order. I have known Mr. McNamara, the Chief Commissioner of the Wheat Board, for many years and have great difficulty believing that he would give this order. I am afraid he must have been pressured into it by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce or somebody who was not familiar with the problem. In any event, Mr. McNamara made this unwise decision as a result of pressure from somebody. The result of the decision was that the pipe line was immediately choked up with wet grain. Anyone who knows the situation in western Canada realizes that we have about 25 million acres of wheat under cultivation. A three-bushel quota means 75 million bushels of wet grain immediately going into what we refer to as the market pipe line.
Mr. McNamara, in his statement of November 28, said that the total drying facilities at all the terminals, Vancouver, Fort William, Lethbridge, Edmonton, Moose Jaw and Saskatoon was only 12 million bushels per month. Is it reasonable for a man in Mr. McNamara's position to make a decision that would mean the moving of 75 million bushels of wet grain into terminals that could not dry a quarter of it? Somebody told the Wheat Board to make this decision, and I would like to find out who it was. I hate to think it was the Wheat Board alone that decided on this action; therefore I ask the question of the minister.
The fifth problem is the serious shortage of box cars and other rolling stock to move grain into market positions, and the resulting large number of grain ships sitting empty in the port of Vancouver. These ships are costing farmers hundreds of thousands of dollars in demurrage charges and a serious loss of grain markets because Canada has been unable to deliver this commodity.
The sixth basic problem, and a prime reason why agriculture is in serious trouble, is

that we have three ministers involved in the affairs of agriculture. It is a case of too many cooks spoiling the broth. I ask, Mr. Speaker, how can one man serve two masters? We have had this problem in the past and this is a case of history repeating itself. In 1958, under the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), whom I had the honour of serving at that time, we had 750 million bushels of grain piled up all over western Canada. When we raised this problem with the then minister of trade and commerce, he said it was the responsibility of the department of agriculture and his department did not have to worry about it. We went to the minister of agriculture, who said the minister of trade and commerce sold the produce of this country.
We did not fool around; we took the Wheat Board from the minister of trade and commerce and placed it under the control of the minister of agriculture, at that time the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, and started to get action. The Wheat Board, which is the body primarily responsible for moving our grain, should be under the jurisdiction of the minister of agriculture. This is where the Wheat Board should be, and it should stay there.
The seventh point, and I think one of the most serious matters in connection with this whole problem, is a psychological one. I have listed these points in numerical order, and because this is the seventh I do not mean it is the least important. As I have said, this is a psychological problem and when you get psychological problems in a depressed area, the over-all problem is aggravated. The problem is that farmers have become very discouraged with the situation because of the inaction of the government. Government action in this field has been too little and too late.
We find the Prime Minister of this country saying in Winnipeg at a $50 a plate dinner for the Liberal party that his government-he said this to the farmers in answer to a question-was not responsible for selling grain and it was up to the farmers to sell it. This was the last straw. After all, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and his department, or somebody in Ottawa, must take the initiative. The farmer cannot himself take it. The inaction of the government has resulted in the serious and difficult situation of western agriculture and is the basic cause of the trouble.

It is all right for me to criticize and enumerate the causes of this problem, but what should we do about it? I feel that the $600 that we are providing now is a start, but it is not enough. It represents about 10 cents a bushel for the farmer who may have grain to market, but the cost of drying his grain amounts to about 20 cents a bushel. An average farmer would have around 10 thousand bushels of grain, and at the cost of 20 cents a bushel he would have to spend about $2,000. The $600 might help, but it does not go far enough.
Some time ago I indicated that we should provide an outright grant in an emergency. At that time I suggested an acreage payment because in 1959 that is what we gave when millions of bushels of grain were under snow. We also did that in 1961 at the time of the emergency to which I referred a while ago. We also used acreage payments on another occasion, but this extra incentive of an outright grant or acreage payment was just enough to give farmers the encouragement they needed and to make them feel we were interested in helping them.
I also suggested on several occasions that we should provide a co-operative plan in conjunction with provincial ministers of agriculture to subsidize the movement of machinery. We did that back in the hungry thirties and also in 1961. We should have done it in this case so that drying equipment would be moved into place. The latest figures show that around 3,200 pieces of drying equipment exist in western Canada but that only 900 are being used. When one starts to question the reason behind that one finds that a large number of farmers have not the wherewithal to pay for transportation to get the dryers into the area where they should be used. As a result, we are losing much valuable time which could be used if equipment were put to work until the end of April, when we are really going to have a serious problem with grain starting to heat. On January 21 I asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) whether additional funds would be made available for vocational training and facilities therefor. He indicated that no additional funds would be allocated for vocational training in technical schools. I then asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on January 24 whether, having in mind his statement that with the elimination

Would he agree that there should be funds allotted for such a purpose, particularly because of the urgency connected with the situation? My question was not accepted and I referred it to the late show.
I should like to refer briefly to some of the statements made in the house by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. In October, the Prime Minister said he had explained that the winter works program would be replaced by programs entailing much higher and much more useful expenditures as far as the economic expansion of the country was concerned. In answer to a question the Prime Minister also said that when the government abandoned the winter works program, it did so because it felt there were other ways in which to ensure prosperity. On September 16 he said that we must terminate any programs which could be replaced by more productive ones, and must defer any which were not immediately essential. I would suggest that in each and every one of these cases those responsible for making the statements were dealing with the upgrading of people going to technical and vocational schools. It put a question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) as to whether additional funds would be available, and he answered "no". I now suggest that an answer should be given in the house as to whether or not the additional funds that were said to be allocated for the upgrading of those people who need this type of training will be provided. It appears that no such funds are available. We realize that there is some difficulty in projecting what will be necessary in the future for the upgrading of certain skills, but I suggest that in these provinces where technical and vocational schools are provided there is a definite need for federal participation in view of the rapid movement of employees in this country.
We all realize that there is a great mobility in our society, and it becomes the federal responsiblity to provide funds to upgrade those people who must move. I suggest there is a real urgency in providing this type of

speechtext:
My
question arises out of one I directed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on January 29 suggesting a possible leak by members of the government caucus with regard to certain proposed changes in the Estate Tax proposal.
If one refers to Hansard at page 4899, one will find that I asked the minister whether he had authorized the hon. member for Pro-vencher (Mr. Smerchanski) and the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Cobbe) to disclose his intention to make certain changes, and bow to some of the opposition to the bill. The minister replied: "No, Mr. Speaker".
The reason I object to that answer is that just by the sheerest coincidence the two hon. members I mentioned had held a press conference at Liberal party headquarters in Winnipeg on the Monday. I am told the hon. member for Portage had appeared on television. And they made statements to the press.
February 4, 1969	COMMONS
I have before me a clipping from the Winnipeg Free Press of January 28, wherein it is stated:
Changes in the proposed estates tax bill are expected to be announced in Ottawa shortly by Finance Minister E. J. Benson, two Manitoba M.P.s disclosed at a Winnipeg press conference.
Gerald R. Cobbe, chairman of the Manitoba federal caucus, and Mark G. Smerchanski said the Canadian Finance Minister had decided to bow to the opposition on the bill that had come up from both within and without the party in recent weeks.
First, they dealt with the matter of exemption, and indicated the exemption figure would probably be made considerably higher. The exact figure of $50,000 was not given, but it was indicated the figure would be considerably higher. In the second place, the press were told the revised proposal would include:
An altered method of paying so that estate taxes could, if necessary, be paid over, say, a five-year period-an annual penalty based on "current interest rates" to be charged.
The report continued:
To eliminate the uncertainty about proposed legislation that would not be retroactive to October, 1968, an arrangement whereby the new tax would only take effect from the date it becomes law. Thus, persons in the process of making decisions regarding their estates until then could have an option of whether they prefer the old or the new legislation.
Other statements were made by the two hon. members, blowing their own horns, to the effect that they had put pressure on the minister, and so forth.
That is just so much barnyard fertilizer, Mr. Speaker. We know there was opposition. There has been opposition by mail. There has been every type of opposition from this side of the house. There has been opposition from backbenchers. Those chaps aren't telling us anything. The minister's own members would tell us that they were opposed to many of these things.
Speeches were made on the subject by members on this side, both inside and outside the house. I have heard speeches made before the tax foundation, assessments of the proposals, and I participated in the discussions. But what I am objecting to is members of the government party claiming that they have influence on the minister and are able to zero in on precisely the three points that were announced by the minister in his press release the following day. The coincidence is very close, and is also very touching.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. B. Osier (Winnipeg South Centre):
maintopic: POWER-NELSON RIVER, MANITOBA-ALLEGED HARMFUL EFFECTS OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question arises because of great concern being felt over something that potentially is very good for northern Manitoba. We have two important rivers, the Nelson and the Churchill, which fall in approximately parallel courses towards Hudson Bay. As is probably well known, it is planned to harness the Nelson River and obtain about 6 million kilowatts of power from it at a cost of about $1 billion. The federal government is taking part in this enterprise by contributing to the cost of 596 odd miles of transmission line south from the power site. This could be a bonanza for the province and for most of us in Canada, but there is another side to the coin which seriously worries me and which has prompted my participation in this debate at this time.
There are experts who are very, very concerned about an Indian community of 100 families who earn an average income of $3,600 a year from trapping, fishing and that sort of thing. That sort of income is very unusual for Indians. These Indians are completely self-sufficient. I believe one man only is on welfare. Everybody else is secure in employment there. The Indians there are in tune with their environment and able to live well.
It is proposed to back up the Churchill River and allow this valley where the Indians live and South Indian Lake to be submerged under 35 feet of water. The Indians living there would have to move away without receiving adequate compensation. There is no sign yet that they will receive adequate compensation. That sort of thing has already happened to one Indian community, and it was ruined by having to move.
The people of Churchill are also concerned about what will happen to them if 80 per cent of the water of the Churchill River is diverted. The federal government is taking some interest in this area. The people there wonder if the river will freeze in the winter. Will there be enough water to service existing sewage facilities? Will shipping be able to come there? Will there be enough water for the whales, and will the whaling industry there survive? Also, will there be enough water to fill existing wells and, as I have already asked, will ships be able to come to the port? I am not a prophet of gloom but I do not believe these questions have been adequately answered by anyone.
February 4, 1969	COMMONS
Another community called Nelson House which consists of 1,200 people is in serious trouble. This community, fairly close to Lake Winnipeg, is in potentially serious trouble. Financial experts feel that, to the Indians at South Indian Lake, their fishing is worth $1,-
171,000	in income, and their trapping is worth $51,000. Those figures might be taken as the basis of any compensation awarded to those people. The industry of the people up there will be ruined because the provincial government will not listen to experts who have looked into the situation. These experts are not spurious or invented. They are real experts whom I can name. A report has been submitted to the provincial government by its own experts. If the government does not listen to them that is its own business, but the loss affects all Manitoba.
The premier of Manitoba says that he will reconsider his decision on the matter. But I am worried in case he is tied to an agreement with the federal government respecting the supply of power lines which may be one of those non-negotiable, non-changeable situations in which the dictates of common sense must be ignored for the sake of a piece of paper. I hope that is not so. From reports I have seen it is indicated that changes that would take place in the development of power, if any of the alternative suggestions proposed by the provincial Hydro authority were accepted, would be infinitesimal when one considers the five or six million kilowatts of power that would be produced by the entire development. Certainly, the proposed changes are not great enough to justify the steps proposed to be taken. Viable alternatives to present courses of action exist. For instance, water needed to produce power could be held or stored in Saskatchewan. It seems, however, that the Manitoba provincial government wants to have control of this water. Other alternatives might be considered. The provincial government might consider taking water from Minnesota or North Dakota. At any rate, we should ask ourselves if we need this water badly enough to dispossess the people I have referred to of their livelihoods.
I hope the federal government is not irrevocably committed to a situation that will allow the provincial government to turn the areas I have spoken of into a swamp that may last for 100 years. In the opinion of ecologists and other experts the swamp will last that long. On the other hand, if the provincial government wishes to hide behind the coat tails of the federal government and do

speakeroldname: Mr. R. J. Orange (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Mines, Energy and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: POWER-NELSON RIVER, MANITOBA-ALLEGED HARMFUL EFFECTS OF DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has been talking about the problems which have been brought about as the result of the growth and development of our country. As any of our important resources are developed people may have to be relocated, or allocated other places to live. Of course, if resources both under the ground and on top of the ground are to be developed there will have to be a relocation of our people.
The hon. member has touched on something that is fundamental to our thinking. He is concerned about the people from Nelson House and South Indian River and is worried that they will be forced to move because of economic development taking place in their area.
I should like to review some of the arrangements which have been made between the federal government and the provincial government of Manitoba with respect to what I consider a magnificent opportunity for economic development in Canada. I am, of course, talking of the transmission line the hon. member mentioned and the development of the Nelson and Churchill Rivers. The federal and provincial governments arranged to-share in the cost of developing the site. Studies included a complete power survey of the Nelson River and a study of the Churchill River diversion as well as alternative routes. The power development project then proceeded into phase 1. This includes a transmission line financed by the federal government, as the Manitoba government was unable to undertake the project by itself. The line will be made available to the province for operation on a lease basis.
Manitoba's responsibilities in phase 1 include the Nelson River generating stations, the Churchill River diversion, and control of the level of Lake Winnipeg. Studies of the Churchill River diversion were undertaken by consulting firms which delved into all aspects of the situation, including the provision of facilities for relocation of families whose lands might be flooded. Under the agreement, Mr. Speaker, this was a provincial responsibility.
The federal government has committed $170 million for the transmission line project. The province has committed $250 million for

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the Nelson River hydroelectric development and the Churchill River diversion.
I say to the hon. member the cost of relocating the people affected will be covered by the province. I am sure the province recognizes this. The financial cost and also the human and economic cost of diversion or relocation of the people involved is the fundamental problem. This problem rests with the province in terms of what happens to the people. I feel sorry for the hundred families of the South Indian Lake area who could be forced off their land. At the moment, this responsibility rests with the provincial government. The federal government has not

made a cost-sharing arrangement with the provincial government in order to proceed with economic development.
